PHP Basics · in Visual Studio Code with XAMPP

Learn PHP by building a small website

Start from an empty folder and build a working website, a few lines at a time. Each short section adds one idea, and you see it work in the browser before moving on.

  • PHP basics: variables, output, decisions, loops and functions
  • A shared layout with includes and a menu that grows by itself
  • Input: GET values from the address bar, and POST forms with checks
  • Sessions: remember a visitor between pages, then a notes list you can add to, update and delete
  • An API: JSON endpoints for GET, POST, PATCH and DELETE, sharing the same session

Try every step here first

From section 1.5 on, each section ends with a Try it simulator: a small editor and browser that run real PHP 8.2 on this page. A tip box points to the line to change and shows the code. It ticks when your code matches, then asks you to run the page and check the result. Stuck? Press Insert for me.

The simulator is for practice. Build the real project in VS Code and XAMPP as well, because that’s what you’ll use for your own work.

How a PHP page works

Every time a browser asks for a page, PHP runs your file from top to bottom and sends back the result. Nothing is remembered between requests unless you store it, which is what sessions are for.

How each section works

  • Each section changes only a few lines. Coloured bars in the code mark new and changed lines, so you can see exactly what to type.
  • NEW FILE means create it. REPLACE WHOLE FILE means select everything in the file and paste over it. You can also just type in the highlighted lines.
  • A comment like // continued in section 9.4: sending the browser to another page marks where code arrives later. Type it in or leave it out: it does nothing.
  • Each section ends with a checkpoint: what you should see in the browser. Every few sections there’s a Your turn challenge.
Tested: all 59 steps of the project were built in order and checked on a real PHP server: every page, form, session change and API request.
1.1 Install XAMPP ›

1.1 · Getting started

Install XAMPP

XAMPP gives you Apache (a web server) and PHP in one installer, so your computer can run PHP pages.

  1. Go to apachefriends.org and download XAMPP for Windows (8.2 or newer).
  2. Run the installer. If Windows warns about antivirus or User Account Control, click OK. Installing to C:\xampp avoids the UAC problem.
  3. Follow the tour below.

Let the terminal find PHP

XAMPP doesn't tell Windows where PHP is. Add it, so you can run php commands in VS Code's terminal:

  1. Press the Start button and type environment variables. Choose Edit environment variables for your account.
  2. Select Path and press Edit…, then New, and type C:\xampp\php. Press OK twice.
  3. Close VS Code completely and open it again, so it picks up the change.
“php is not recognized”? The terminal was opened before you changed Path. Close every VS Code window and try again.

1.6 · Getting started

Your first line of PHP

Now add some PHP. Code between <?php and ?> runs on the server before the page is sent.

Files in this section
  • Updatehello.php

What’s new

  • <?php starts PHP mode and ?> ends it.
  • echo prints text into the page. Here it prints some HTML.
  • Every statement ends with a semicolon ;
  • Lines starting with // are comments: notes for people, ignored by PHP.
Checkpoint: run the app
Save, then open hello.php. Right-click › View page source. You’ll see “Hello from PHP!” but no PHP code: the browser only gets the result.
Never put ?> in a comment A ?> ends PHP mode, even inside a // comment. Everything after it is shown on the page as plain text.

2.1 · Variables

Your first variable

A variable is a named box that holds a value. In PHP every variable name starts with $.

  1. Make a new file called variables.php.
Files in this section
  • Newvariables.php

What’s new

  • $name = 'Sam'; puts the text Sam into a box called $name.
  • Text (a string) goes in quotes.
  • PHP code can sit at the top of the file, above the HTML.
  • The short tag <?= $name ?> prints a value inside the HTML. It’s short for <?php echo $name; ?>.
Checkpoint: run the app
Save, then open variables.php. It says “Hello, Sam!”. Change 'Sam' to your own name, save and refresh.

‹ 3.2 printf and number_format3.4 Printing safely ›

3.4 · Output

Printing safely

This is the most important rule in this guide: never print what a visitor typed without escaping it first.

Files in this section
  • Updateoutput.php

What’s new

  • $comment pretends to be something a visitor typed, with a sneaky <script> in it.
  • htmlspecialchars() turns < into &lt; and so on, so the browser shows the code instead of running it.
Why it matters: without escaping, anyone could put JavaScript on your page that runs in other visitors’ browsers. This is called cross-site scripting (XSS).
Checkpoint: run the app
Save, then open output.php. The “Safe” line shows the script tag as text, and no alert box pops up.

4.3 · Decisions and loops

Loops with foreach

A loop repeats code. foreach runs once for every item in an array.

Files in this section
  • Updateloops.php

Reading the search box

Anything after ? in an address is a query string. PHP puts it in $_GET. A form with method="get" puts its fields there.

Files in this section
  • Updatesearch.php
MethodMeansIn this guide
GETRead something. Values go in the address: ?q=laneSearch books, list notes, load a note
POSTSend data to create or change something. Values go in the request body.Contact form, add a note, sign in
PATCH / PUTUpdate something that already existsMark a note as done through the API
DELETERemove somethingDelete a note through the API

What’s new

  • The search box shows what was searched for, escaped with e().

‹ 8.4 Checking the other fields9.1 Starting a session ›

9.1 · Sessions

Starting a session

Each request starts from nothing. A session lets PHP remember things about one visitor between requests.

  1. Make a new file called profile.php.
Files in this section
  • Updateincludes/init.php
  • Newprofile.php

How it works

  1. session_start() gives the visitor an ID, sent to the browser in a cookie called PHPSESSID.
  2. The browser sends that cookie back with every request.
  3. PHP uses it to load that visitor’s $_SESSION array, which is kept on the server.

What’s new

  • session_start() goes in init.php, so every page has a session. It must run before any HTML is sent.
  • profile.php counts how many times you’ve opened it.
Checkpoint: run the app
Save, then open profile.php. Refresh a few times: the number goes up. It survives between requests because it’s stored in your session.
Try another browser Open the same page in a different browser or a private window. It starts from 1: a different cookie means a different session.

  • HTML forms can only send GET or POST, so the hidden action field says update.

‹ 10.6 Ticking a note as done11.1 A JSON endpoint ›

11.1 · API

A JSON endpoint

An endpoint is an address that sends back data instead of a web page. Yours sends the notes as JSON.

  1. Make a folder called api, and inside it notes.php. In the main folder, make notes.http.
Files in this section
  • Newapi/notes.php
  • Updateincludes/notes.php
  • Newnotes.http

What’s new

  • header('Content-Type: application/json') says it’s data, not HTML.
  • respond() turns any PHP value into JSON with json_encode, sets the status code and stops.
  • It loads init.php and includes/notes.php, so it uses the same session and functions as the Notes page.
Session passthrough Your browser sends the same PHPSESSID cookie to notes.php and api/notes.php. So the API sees exactly the notes you added on the page.
Checkpoint: run the app
Save, then open api/notes.php. Add a note on the Notes page first, then open the API in the same browser: your notes, as JSON.

Try it with REST Client

  1. Open notes.http. A small Send Request link appears above the request.
  2. Click it. The reply opens on the right: 200 OK and [].
  3. Why empty? REST Client has its own cookies, so it’s a different visitor with its own session.

‹ 10.7 Deleting a note11.2 POST: adding a note ›

11.2 · API

POST: adding a note

Callers send a new note as JSON in the request body.

Files in this section
  • Updateapi/notes.php
  • Updatenotes.http

What’s new

  • jsonBody() reads php://input and decodes it.
  • It refuses anything that isn’t JSON (415) or isn’t valid (400).
  • Bad data gets 422 with the same messages as the web form. Success gets 201 Created.
CodeMeans
200 OKIt worked
201 CreatedA new thing was made
400 Bad RequestThe request didn’t make sense
404 Not FoundNo such note
415 Unsupported Media TypeIt wasn’t sent as JSON
422 UnprocessableThe data failed the checks
Checkpoint: run the app
In REST Client, send request 2 (201), then request 1 again: the note is there. Request 5 gives 422.
Why insist on JSON? Another website can’t send Content-Type: application/json with your visitor’s cookie without your server agreeing first. That protects the API the way the CSRF token protects forms.

12.1 · Wrap up

Security checklist and next steps

The habits you've practised

HabitWhere you used it
Escape every output with e() / htmlspecialchars()Every page that prints user input
Validate every input on the servercontact.php, notes.php, the API
Use filter_input or casts for numberssearch.php, notes.php
POST for changes, GET for readingForms, sign out, the API
A CSRF token on forms that change thingsnotes.php
Post/Redirect/Get after a successful formwelcome.php, notes.php
A new session ID when someone signs in or outwelcome.php, logout.php
declare(strict_types=1)functions.php

Where to go next

  • Databases: store notes in MySQL with PDO and prepared statements, so they last for ever and are shared.
  • Real logins: password_hash() and password_verify() for passwords.
  • Composer: PHP’s package manager.
  • A framework: when you’re comfortable, Laravel does routing, sessions, validation and CSRF for you. The Laravel guide in the Tutorial Library picks up from here.
‹ 11.7 PATCH and DELETE buttons12.2 Troubleshooting ›

12.2 · Wrap up

Troubleshooting

You seeWhat to do
The browser downloads the .php file, or shows your codeYou opened the file directly (the address starts with file://). Open it through http://localhost/php-basics/, with Apache running.
Part of your code appears on the pageA ?> ended PHP mode early, often inside a comment (1.6).
A blank white pageA fatal error with errors hidden. In C:\xampp\php\php.ini set display_errors=On (for learning only), restart Apache. Or check C:\xampp\apache\logs\error.log.
Parse error: syntax error, unexpected …Usually a missing ; or bracket on the line before the one it names.
Warning: Undefined array key "q"Use $_GET['q'] ?? '' so a missing value has a default (7.3).
Cannot modify header information - headers already sentSomething was printed before session_start(), header() or redirect(). Check for spaces or blank lines before <?php, and for a closing ?> at the end of include files.
Failed to open stream: No such file or directoryThe path in require is wrong. Use __DIR__ . '/includes/…' and check the spelling and folder.
TypeError: … must be of type string, int givenStrict types caught a mismatch. Pass the right type, or cast it: (string) $x.
The session forgets everythingIs session_start() running on every page (via init.php)? Are cookies allowed? A private window starts a new session.
“This form has expired” (419)The CSRF token didn’t match. Refresh the page and try again.
REST Client gets 404Check @base matches how you run the site: XAMPP or php -S (11.1).
Apache won’t start: “Port 80 in use”Another program has the port (often Skype or IIS). Close it, or use php -S localhost:8000 instead.
